The Cerro Bandera Formation is 45 m-thick and consists\r\nof pyroclastic deposits showing evidence of fluvial rework- ing and/or pedogenesis, alternating with primary fall-out pyroclastic deposits, with abundant bentonitic horizons in the lower section and scant intercalated sandstones in the upper section. The abundant tuffaceous and tuffitic con- tents would have originated from discontinuous ash fall derived from Andean or sub-Andean volcanic centers. The origin of these deposits is associated with a fluvial environ- ment in an intermontane foreland basin; lacustrine deposits accumulated in the central, topographically lower areas of the paleovalleys, whereas paleosols accumulated in the marginal, higher areas. This depositional system resulted in marked lateral facies variations among the currently isolated exposures (Leanza and Hugo, 1997; Kramarz et al., 2005). Several

identified_name: Megapiranha paranensis n. gen. n. sp.
geogcomments:
The specimen comes from the well known late Miocene fossil vertebrate locality along the Rio Parana near the city of Parana, Entre Rios, Argentina. 

Unfortunately, most of the fossils in collections from the Parana area do not include adequate provenance. Labels in collections usually only state that the material comes from the base of the cliffs near Parana. However, recent field work has confirmed that almost all of the Miocene terrestrial and freshwater aquatic vertebrates come from the “Conglomerado Osifero”at the base of the Ituzaingo Formation.

The material here described comes from the “Conglomerado osifero” of the Ituzaingo Formation. The holotype (MLP 96-XI- 5-1) was collected by Santiago Roth at the beginning of the 20th century in an indeterminate locality between the cities of Parana ́ and Villa Urquiza, Entre Rios (Fig. 1). Additional material includes an isolated tooth (CICYTTP-PV-P-1-125) from the Conglomerado osifero cropping out in the base of the Parana riverside eastern cliffs in the SLC1 (Colonia La Celina, Entre Rios) by Jorge Casciotta, Alberto Cione, Jorge Noriega and Leopoldo Soibelzon in June, 1999.

Six sections of the Chenque Formation were studied palynologically. These sections are located in the east-central part of the San Jorge Basin, located in the southeastern and northeastern extreme of Chubut and Santa Cruz provinces respectively in Patagonia. Three of these sections (Chenque Hill, Viteau Hill and "Antena" Hill) are near Comodoro Rivadavia, S. Jorge basin, eastern Patagonia. This city, located at latitude 45º47´S and longitude 67º 30´W, was built at the foot of Chenque Hill. Viteau Hill and "Antena" Hill" are located approximately 3 km northwest of Chenque Hill. The Cañadón Baumann section is located about 25.5 km north-northwest of Punta Borja, Comodoro Rivadavia. Other two small sections, Punta Delgada and Playa Las Cuevas, are located on the Atlantic coast, 16.5 km and 21 km, respectively, away from Punta Borja (Comodoro Rivadavia).

Three of these sections (Chenque Hill, Viteau Hill and "Antena" Hill) are near Comodoro Rivadavia, S. Jorge basin, eastern Patagonia. This city, located at latitude 45º47´S and longitude 67º 30´W, was built at the foot of Chenque Hill. Viteau Hill and "Antena" Hill" are located approximately 3 km northwest of Chenque Hill. The Cañadón Baumann section is located about 25.5 km north-northwest of Punta Borja, Comodoro Rivadavia. Other two small sections, Punta Delgada and Playa Las Cuevas, are located on the Atlantic coast, 16.5 km and 21 km, respectively, away from Punta Borja (Comodoro Rivadavia).

It is in the intertidal zone (?S51°, 3.220;W69°, 8.300),\r\n3.3 km north of the entrance to the beach at Estancia La Costa (ELC) (Fig. 2A). Named for a large slump on the cliff above the fossiliferous beach exposures, the locality consists of two areas of exposure separated by a north- east–southwest cross-bedded channel sandstone. The southern exposure is approximately 8.5 ha in extent and the northern exposure is approximately 1.0 ha, as deter- mined by GPS. This fossil locality has the greatest surface exposure of any along the coast between Coy inlet and Cabo Buen Tiempo and, unlike any of the others, all the fossils come from the same horizon. The southern margin of the exposure disappears into beach silt; a low scarp sculpted by marine erosion delimits the northern edge of the exposure.

"This locality was omitted in the letter that Carlos Ameghino sent to his brother Florentino on May 6, 1887. However, his Travel Diary mentions that he found an important fossiliferous site, which he informally called Segundas Barrancas Blancas, located West of Barrancas Blancas and East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). Carlos did not use that name in his 1890 publication, but he gave further geographical details to locate this fossiliferous locality slightly West of Basalt Glen and about 45 km East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). The different geographical references of the three accounts are com- plementary. We locate an extensive outcrop of about 14 km in length from East (S 50 16012.4800 e W 70 22023.2100 W) to West (S 50 16051.90 00 e W 70 17054.7600). The western end of this exposure is located at Ea. Cordón Alto, while the eastern end is at Ea. Rincon Grande (Topographic Chart Estancia La Barrancosa, 5169-1). The exposures lie at the bottom of the valley, where the river erodes its southern slope."

Named for a large slump on the cliff above the fossiliferous beach exposures, the locality consists of two areas of exposure separated by a north- east–southwest cross-bedded channel sandstone. The southern exposure is approximately 8.5 ha in extent and the northern exposure is approximately 1.0 ha, as deter- mined by GPS. This fossil locality has the greatest surface exposure of any along the coast between Coy inlet and Cabo Buen Tiempo and, unlike any of the others, all the fossils come from the same horizon. The southern margin of the exposure disappears into beach silt; a low scarp sculpted by marine erosion delimits the northern edge of the exposure.

Locality is unclear. Sterli and de la Fuente (2011) provide the following information: "The confusion regarding the locality and age of Nio. argentina also stems from the dispute between Moreno and Ameghino. Ameghino (1899:10) mentions that the turtle remains came from the “Formacion guaranitica del Sehuen y del Chubut” (Guaranitic Formation from Sehuen and Chubut), but Woodward (1901) mentions that Roth collected extinct reptiles in association with mammals from the “red sandstone, supposed to be of Cretaceous age” (Woodward, 1901:169). To make matters even more confusing, Ameghino (1906) pointed out that Roth’s locality is located three kilometers northwest of Colhue-Huapı Lake (now known as Muster Lake) in outcrops yielding a Notostylops fauna, which is identified within the Casamayoran SALMA (Middle Eocene). The Museo de La Plata collection label accompanying the remains of Nio. argentina mentions the locality as Canadon Blanco and the age as Cretaceous. However, the exact location of the Canadon Blanco locality found by Roth cannot be determined, other than that it is somewhere within Chubut Province, Argentina. Furthermore, the mammalian fauna found at the Canadon Blanco locality indicates that the locality is Eocene to Early Oligocene in age (45–22 Ma) (Simpson, 1967; Reguero et al., 2003). Further preparation of an Nio. argentina skull allowed us to recover sediments from its nasal cavity. The sediment is a white, poorly consolidated tuff, inconsistent with Woodward’s (1901:169) claim that the material was found in a Cretaceous “red sandstone.” However, the Sarmiento Formation (25 Ma; Eocene–Miocene) (Bellosi, 2010) in Chubut Province is dominated by a similar white tuff, indicating an Eocene–Miocene age for the Nio. argentina neotype". Given the geographic and temporal uncertainty, the occurrence of Nio. argentina is added to a separate locality to avoid mixing and confusion with the other records of Canadon Blanco in the PBDB that are more precisely located.

Historical background. This locality was first introduced by Goin et al. (1994: fig. 1).\r\nOutcrop description. The “Irenean” deposits are exposed along about 100 m of the right margin and 80 m of the left margin; the outcrop coincides with a tufa barrier of about 70 m in length that crossed the Quequén Salado River diagonally, producing a cascade with a fall of about 1.5 m.

Historical background. This locality was first introduced by Goin et al. (1994: fig. 1).\r\nOutcrop description. The “Irenean” deposits are exposed along about 100 m of the right margin and 80 m of the left margin; the outcrop coincides with a tufa barrier of about 70 m in length that crossed the Quequén Salado River diagonally, producing a cascade with a fall of about 1.5 m.

Historical background. The first mention of this locality using a proper name is credited to Fidalgo et al. (1975, p. 125) yet Mignone (1949) was the first author to describe and figure stratigraphic profiles in Cascada Grande, although he did not identify the waterfall by name. Fidalgo et al. (1975, p. 119) published a schematic column that putatively reflects the stratigraphic sequence in this locality. Schillizzi et al. (2005, p. 96) figured a stratigraphic profile at Cascada Grande, where the lower portion was referred to the “Irene Formation” and several structures including the ichnofossil Coprinisphaera (see also Cantil et al., 2013). Rasia and Candela (2013: fig. 2) provided a stratigraphic profile of Cascada Grande based on the unpublished notes of Pardiñas and Lezcano deposited at the MLP. Isla et al. (2014: fig. 5) mentioned the locality, as Cascada Cifuentes, and figured a very schematic profile. \r\n\r\nOutcrop description (Fig. 3). This locality is distinguished by an important waterfall, the highest in the Province of Buenos Aires (4 m high). This waterfall was formed by the collapse of a tufa dam, 325 m downstream, by a catastrophic flooding in early 1980. The “Irenean” exposures extend upstream (180 m by right margin, 150 m by left margin) and downstream (260 m by right margin, 320 m by left margin) of the waterfall.

Historical background. This locality was first mentioned and briefly described by Isla et al. (2014, p. 5). Some specimens of historical collections are labeled as “Indio Rico”, according to Verzi et al. (2003, 2008), and were probably unearthed in the same place.\r\n\r\nOutcrop description (Figs. 5, 6). The outcrop is marked by the existence of a rural road that crossed the stream using a calcrete bank on the stream floor. The “Irenean” fauna is found in sediments exposed along about 100 m on both margins of the Indio Rico Stream; on the left margin, there is also an additional deposit of about 30 m (Fig. 6).

Historical background. We detected this site in 1995 and briefly addressed it in Pardiñas et al. (1996: fig. 1). It was mistakenly referred by Abello (2007, p. 46) as the locality where a specimen of Pliolestes (MLP 94-II-I-120) was collected; the material had been actually found in Paso del Halcón (see below).\r\n\r\nOutcrop description (Fig. 7). It is an isolated sedimentary “patch” with “Irenean” fauna of about 20 m in length on the left margin of the Quequén Salado River and completely “surrounded” by Pleistocene deposits. The place is marked by an important cascade about 2 m tall.

Historical background. Even though we detected this site in 1995, the first mention of the site occurs in this work. Some materials unearthed in this locality were erroneously labeled as coming from Paso de la Tufa when housed at MLP collections (see above).\r\n\r\nOutcrops description (Fig. 7). The sediments bearing “Irenean” assemblages are exposed exclusively on the left margin along about 120 m. In contrast with the other localities herein discussed, Paso del Halcón is characterized by a terraced development covering about 50 m in width and with 3 main levels instead of a classical vertical cliff. Another difference with the other localities is that this outcrop is not associated with a cascade.

Historical background. Paso del Médano is the name of a historical place that was used to cross the Quequén Salado River and as transit area since, at least, colonial times. Its first mention in the paleontological literature is credited to Frenguelli (1928, p. 30). Posteriorly, it was repeatedly mentioned in the literature (e.g., Pascual and Herrera, 1973; Goin et al., 1994; Verzi et al., 2008).

Outcrops description (Fig. 8). To date, the local outcrops from which “Irenean” fossils were exhumed are almost lost due to human modifications (see below). When we made our first visit to this locality, in 1992, we found exposed fossiliferous deposits exclusively on the right margin and covering about 130 m in length. We also detected “Irenean” sediments in tabular banks forming the riverbed to the right of the talweg.

The outcrops, 14 km apart, are exposed over the eastern flank of a NW-SE syncline, in southern Mendoza: Arroyo Durazno (c. 260 m; 35° 5′ S; 69° 45′ W), located over the left margin of the El Durazno Creek, to the south, and Arroyo Paulino (c. 220 m; 34° 58′ S; 69° 49′ W), cropping out on the right margin of the Paulino Creek, to the north. Both localities are accessed through the National Route 40 heading Malargüe City and then following country roads that fork to the west (Fig. 1B). Main geological features of the area were studied by Ugarte (1955), Dessanti (1978) and Nullo et al.  (2005).

Las Hornillas (32º00’S and 69º 45’W) at the Puesto de Gendarmería «Álvarez Condarco», is located 65 km southwest from the village of Barreal (Calingasta Department, San Juan Province; Fig. 1). 
Two diverse fossil mammal assemblages have been recognized along the Los Patos valley, in this area (Table 1). 
One of them found mostly at the right margin of the Los Patos river in the lowest bearing horizon is informally named «Chinches bearing level» (CBL) 
The other, stratigraphically higher and exposed at the left margin of the river, is informally named «Las Hornillas bearing level» (LHBL) (Fig. 2).

It is in the intertidal zone (?S51°, 3.220;W69°, 8.300),\r\n3.3 km north of the entrance to the beach at Estancia La Costa (ELC) (Fig. 2A). Named for a large slump on the cliff above the fossiliferous beach exposures, the locality consists of two areas of exposure separated by a north- east–southwest cross-bedded channel sandstone. The southern exposure is approximately 8.5 ha in extent and the northern exposure is approximately 1.0 ha, as deter- mined by GPS. This fossil locality has the greatest surface exposure of any along the coast between Coy inlet and Cabo Buen Tiempo and, unlike any of the others, all the fossils come from the same horizon. The southern margin of the exposure disappears into beach silt; a low scarp sculpted by marine erosion delimits the northern edge of the exposure.

The specimen comes from the well known late Miocene fossil vertebrate locality along the Rio Parana near the city of Parana, Entre Rios, Argentina. 

Unfortunately, most of the fossils in collections from the Parana area do not include adequate provenance. Labels in collections usually only state that the material comes from the base of the cliffs near Parana. However, recent field work has confirmed that almost all of the Miocene terrestrial and freshwater aquatic vertebrates come from the “Conglomerado Osifero”at the base of the Ituzaingo Formation.

The material here described comes from the “Conglomerado osifero” of the Ituzaingo Formation. The holotype (MLP 96-XI- 5-1) was collected by Santiago Roth at the beginning of the 20th century in an indeterminate locality between the cities of Parana ́ and Villa Urquiza, Entre Rios (Fig. 1). Additional material includes an isolated tooth (CICYTTP-PV-P-1-125) from the Conglomerado osifero cropping out in the base of the Parana riverside eastern cliffs in the SLC1 (Colonia La Celina, Entre Rios) by Jorge Casciotta, Alberto Cione, Jorge Noriega and Leopoldo Soibelzon in June, 1999.

Hatcher (1900, 1903) refers to the area of Lago Posadas, i.e., between the Río Furioso to the west, and Río Tarde to the east (Fig. 1), as “Lake Pueyrredon”.

Hatcher climbed the cliffs of the eastern end of what he first called “Lake Princeton”, but time after recognized that the name Pueyrredón had priority (Hatcher, 1903). Detailed descriptions of the geography and geology of the area by Hatcher allow confirming that the exposures he visited are the same as that we describe in this work (Fig. 2). There Hatcher made a collection of vertebrate fossils from the beds he called the “Santa Cruzian formation” (Hatcher, 1903).

"This locality was omitted in the letter that Carlos Ameghino sent to his brother Florentino on May 6, 1887. However, his Travel Diary mentions that he found an important fossiliferous site, which he informally called Segundas Barrancas Blancas, located West of Barrancas Blancas and East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). Carlos did not use that name in his 1890 publication, but he gave further geographical details to locate this fossiliferous locality slightly West of Basalt Glen and about 45 km East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). The different geographical references of the three accounts are com- plementary. We locate an extensive outcrop of about 14 km in length from East (S 50 16012.4800 e W 70 22023.2100 W) to West (S 50 16051.90 00 e W 70 17054.7600). The western end of this exposure is located at Ea. Cordón Alto, while the eastern end is at Ea. Rincon Grande (Topographic Chart Estancia La Barrancosa, 5169-1). The exposures lie at the bottom of the valley, where the river erodes its southern slope."

The specimen comes from the well known late Miocene fossil vertebrate locality along the Rio Parana near the city of Parana, Entre Rios, Argentina. 

Unfortunately, most of the fossils in collections from the Parana area do not include adequate provenance. Labels in collections usually only state that the material comes from the base of the cliffs near Parana. However, recent field work has confirmed that almost all of the Miocene terrestrial and freshwater aquatic vertebrates come from the “Conglomerado Osifero”at the base of the Ituzaingo Formation.

The material here described comes from the “Conglomerado osifero” of the Ituzaingo Formation. The holotype (MLP 96-XI- 5-1) was collected by Santiago Roth at the beginning of the 20th century in an indeterminate locality between the cities of Parana ́ and Villa Urquiza, Entre Rios (Fig. 1). Additional material includes an isolated tooth (CICYTTP-PV-P-1-125) from the Conglomerado osifero cropping out in the base of the Parana riverside eastern cliffs in the SLC1 (Colonia La Celina, Entre Rios) by Jorge Casciotta, Alberto Cione, Jorge Noriega and Leopoldo Soibelzon in June, 1999.

The specimen comes from the well known late Miocene fossil vertebrate locality along the Rio Parana near the city of Parana, Entre Rios, Argentina. 

Unfortunately, most of the fossils in collections from the Parana area do not include adequate provenance. Labels in collections usually only state that the material comes from the base of the cliffs near Parana. However, recent field work has confirmed that almost all of the Miocene terrestrial and freshwater aquatic vertebrates come from the “Conglomerado Osifero”at the base of the Ituzaingo Formation.

Herrera et al. 2021: The material here studied comes from the Arroyo Paulino section (34 580 S; 69 490 W), which is around 220 m thick and encompass upper Tithonian to lower Berriasian strata of the Vaca Muerta Formation cropping out on the right margin of the Paulino Creek, Malargüe, Mendoza. Arroyo Paulino can be reached following upstream a country-road that departs to the west from the 40 National Road and that parallels the course of the Atuel River and its tributaries (Fig. 1A). General geological features of the area have been published by Ugarte (1955), Dessanti (1978), Nullo et al. (2005), and Sruoga et al. (2005), and a detailed complete log of the section is available in Fernandez et al. (2019).

An old Ameghino locality relocated by Fernicola et al. (2014). 

"This locality was omitted in the letter that Carlos Ameghino sent to his brother Florentino on May 6, 1887. However, his Travel Diary mentions that he found an important fossiliferous site, which he informally called Segundas Barrancas Blancas, located West of Barrancas Blancas and East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). Carlos did not use that name in his 1890 publication, but he gave further geographical details to locate this fossiliferous locality slightly West of Basalt Glen and about 45 km East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). The different geographical references of the three accounts are com- plementary. We locate an extensive outcrop of about 14 km in length from East (S 50 16012.4800 e W 70 22023.2100 W) to West (S 50 16051.90 00 e W 70 17054.7600). The western end of this exposure is located at Ea. Cordón Alto, while the eastern end is at Ea. Rincon Grande (Topographic Chart Estancia La Barrancosa, 5169-1). The exposures lie at the bottom of the valley, where the river erodes its southern slope."

Arnal et al 2019: This is a belt of 9 km of exposures composed of several isolated outcrops that lie close to the Río Santa Cruz in Estancia Cordón Alto and Estancia El Tordillo (Figs. 1, 9, and 10). Here we measured five sections (Fig. 11), which from east to west are: Estancia El Tordillo 2 (EET2; S 50° 16’ 39.08”; W 70° 13’ 26.18”), Estancia El Tordillo 1 (EET1; S50° 16’ 43.00”; W 70° 15’ 9.90”), Estancia Cordón Alto 2 (ECA2; S 50° 16’ 55.96”; W 70° 15’ 47.33”), Estancia Cordón Alto 1 (ECA1; S 50° 16’ 25.56”; W 70° 18’ 24.74”), and Point 9 (S 50° 16’ 16.30”; W 70° 20’ 48.60”) (Figs. 9 and 11). In each of these sections vertebrate fossils were recovered (Fernicola et al., 2019b).

"This locality was omitted in the letter that Carlos Ameghino sent to his brother Florentino on May 6, 1887. However, his Travel Diary mentions that he found an important fossiliferous site, which he informally called Segundas Barrancas Blancas, located West of Barrancas Blancas and East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). Carlos did not use that name in his 1890 publication, but he gave further geographical details to locate this fossiliferous locality slightly West of Basalt Glen and about 45 km East of Yaten Huageno (Fig. 2). The different geographical references of the three accounts are com- plementary. We locate an extensive outcrop of about 14 km in length from East (S 50 16012.4800 e W 70 22023.2100 W) to West (S 50 16051.90 00 e W 70 17054.7600). The western end of this exposure is located at Ea. Cordón Alto, while the eastern end is at Ea. Rincon Grande (Topographic Chart Estancia La Barrancosa, 5169-1). The exposures lie at the bottom of the valley, where the river erodes its southern slope."

Historical background. The first mention of this locality using a proper name is credited to Fidalgo et al. (1975, p. 125) yet Mignone (1949) was the first author to describe and figure stratigraphic profiles in Cascada Grande, although he did not identify the waterfall by name. Fidalgo et al. (1975, p. 119) published a schematic column that putatively reflects the stratigraphic sequence in this locality. Schillizzi et al. (2005, p. 96) figured a stratigraphic profile at Cascada Grande, where the lower portion was referred to the “Irene Formation” and several structures including the ichnofossil Coprinisphaera (see also Cantil et al., 2013). Rasia and Candela (2013: fig. 2) provided a stratigraphic profile of Cascada Grande based on the unpublished notes of Pardiñas and Lezcano deposited at the MLP. Isla et al. (2014: fig. 5) mentioned the locality, as Cascada Cifuentes, and figured a very schematic profile. \r\n\r\nOutcrop description (Fig. 3). This locality is distinguished by an important waterfall, the highest in the Province of Buenos Aires (4 m high). This waterfall was formed by the collapse of a tufa dam, 325 m downstream, by a catastrophic flooding in early 1980. The “Irenean” exposures extend upstream (180 m by right margin, 150 m by left margin) and downstream (260 m by right margin, 320 m by left margin) of the waterfall.

The Cerro Buitre Norte (CBN) section (base at S42.97034, W67.54350, WGS84 datum) is the primary stratigraphic section studied here. The Cerro Buitre Norte section (also known colloquially as the “Plesiosaurio” section) represents one of the longest and most continuous exposures of the La Colonia Formation in the region, especially for the middle-upper parts of the unit. The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The Cerro Buitre Norte (CBN) section (base at S42.97034, W67.54350, WGS84 datum) is the primary stratigraphic section studied here. The Cerro Buitre Norte section (also known colloquially as the “Plesiosaurio” section) represents one of the longest and most continuous exposures of the La Colonia Formation in the region, especially for the middle-upper parts of the unit. The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The Cerro Buitre Norte (CBN) section (base at S42.97034, W67.54350, WGS84 datum) is the primary stratigraphic section studied here. The Cerro Buitre Norte section (also known colloquially as the “Plesiosaurio” section) represents one of the longest and most continuous exposures of the La Colonia Formation in the region, especially for the middle-upper parts of the unit. The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

The lower 125 m of the Cerro Buitre Norte section was sampled for this study and spans the middle-upper La Colonia and lower Cerro Bororó formations. The contact between the La Colonia and Cerro Bororó formations occurs at the 108-m level in the section and is marked by a distinct red bed at the top of the La Colonia Formation suggesting slowed deposition or a hiatus of some duration at that time. The Cerro Buitre Norte section is located ~2 km to the southeast of the sections “Norte de Cerro Bayo 1” and “Norte Cerro Bayo 2” presented in Gasparini et al. (2015).

Bahia Nueva, Chubut province, Argentina. Cione (1988), is the first author that recognized that the type specimens of E. pozzii came from Bahía Nueva (as can be seen in the label of the type specimens). Cione suggests that this locality is located between the Chubut River valley and Trelew city (Cione, 1988). However, the port of Bahia Nueva, also known as "de las Ollas" port by the end of the 19th century, corresponds to the coastal area of Puerto Madryn (see Caviglia, 2011). Consequently, the type locality of Echinorhinus pozzii should be considered as the neighborhood of Puerto Madryn city.
